analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "That's correct. That's correct. Only lands that would come in under this Act 289. The Act, for example, has a value for a present purpose of $100,000, and it's up to the capital of the ownership of the police, let's say for a 20-year lease. The tax on that, as we see, the city tax rate is tied to $300,000. Lumped in with a whole assessment valuation. Whatever. Yes. If another 20-year lease on a property that is a million dollars, if you include it, then the left to be there, and for those people, even though we all have a 20-year lease, a higher taxable taxable, then the fellow who has the property that we have that number of money? That's a very important question of the amount of property he's using. Mr. O'Connor, do you have two roles there? Do you have a personal property role and a real property tax role? Yes, we do, Mr. Justice Warren. Then how does this get on your real property role? I notice this exhibit says, The personal property assessment role. Now, that's different. How do you put it on the formal reviewer and then put it on your real property? For lack of a better place to put it, I would give as the answer, we used this and noted on this role, Leased Land Building, Act 189, PA 1953, to distinguish the properties on this role from properties that would be on the general personal property assessment role and subject to the general personal property assessment taxes. We merely used this form and placed on this form that notation. And that notation also was included in the bill, tax bill, that was sent to the lessee so that he was, he could not possibly, under, by any stretch of the imagination, conclude that this was on the personal property assessment role subject to general personal property assessment laws. Well, then is this a third kind of role? You have your real estate role and you have your personal property tax role, and is this a third kind of tax role? Uh, you might call it that, Your Honor. The act was new, and when we were starting to— I'm not criticizing it, I'm just trying to find out what I wanted to ask you, because I should maybe have understood you, but I didn't. I do want to know if these pieces of property that are on this exhibit, 97, are included in your real property role for the purpose of fixing your real property rate. They are, Your Honor. They are. All right, that's all. Is this another way of getting at it, Mr. O'Connor? Let's take the first one, this Borg-Warner. If Borg-Warner owned that property, instead of leasing it, but actually owned it, it would have an assessment as owner of $352,060, wouldn't it? Right. And it would have a tax bill at the tax rate against the $352,000. That's correct. And the tax bill would be a real estate tax bill, wouldn't it? If it owned the property. With this notation contained there. No, no, no. I'm assuming a different case. Assuming it owned the property. Not least it, but owned it. That's correct, Mr. Justice. It would get a real estate tax bill and an assessment of $352,000 at the local rate. Is that so? That's correct. Now, because it's the lessee of the property, it gets what? A different kind of tax bill, a different color maybe or something? I think, frankly, they're using the same bills that they've used in connection with the general personal property tax bill. Yes. With this notation contained on it. It gets a tax bill. It gets a, whatever it may be called, it's still a tax bill and an assessment of $352,060 at the local rate for 1954. That's correct, Your Honor. And, of course, as I have previously said, the value of the United States property may be used as a measure of a tax and privilege under the cases I have cited in my brief and, I believe, mentioned a short while ago. Have you cited any of the interstate commerce cases which have held that immune interstate trade can have a tax levied against it measured by the total value of the interstate trade? No, Mr. Justice Black, I have not. But I have cited Plummer v. Kohler, for example, which is an inheritance or succession tax, which uses the full value of the United States bonds, which were included in the estate, as a measure of the tax of the inheritance or succession tax. And the court concluded, this court concluded, that that tax was not on the bonds of the United States, which were exempt from taxation, but is on the privilege of inheritance or succession. Now, in connection with the home insurance company case, which is a New York case, that involved a franchise tax measured by the dividends and capital stock of the corporation. Included in the capital stock of the corporation included in the capital stock of the corporation were United States bonds, which, of course, were tax exempt. They were included as a measure, the value of those bonds, along with the other properties of the corporation, were included as a measure of the tax on the franchise, which the court said could be done. It was not a tax on the bond. It was not a tax on the bonds, but on the franchise, the privilege of the company conducting business. Is the only challenge to your tax on the basis of it being excessive by reason of the way it's measured, or is the only challenge to it based on immunity? The only challenge is based on immunity. Because the argument is, it's like Miller and Milwaukee. Now, what do you do with that? Well, Miller versus Milwaukee, if your honor please, the tax, the Miller owned dividends in a Milwaukee corporation. The Wisconsin statute provided for a tax on everything except United States bonds. They were accepted from the privilege tax, in that case, in measuring the privilege tax. When the dividends were paid out to Mr. Miller, the stockholder, the Wisconsin statute further provided that he should be taxed on those dividends only to the extent of the United States bonds, the value of the United States bonds. And the court held, and rightfully so in that case, if your honor please, that that statute was specifically aimed at the United States bonds. Now, of course, that case did not involve, as I recall, a franchise or privilege tax. Yes, the Miller case did not involve a franchise or privilege tax, but an income tax. Now, McAllen versus Massachusetts, which government counsel cited in their brief as controlling of the situation, the statute accepted interest from United States bonds in determining net income for purposes of measuring the franchise tax on domestic corporations. The statute was later amended to include tax-exempt securities in the measure of the franchise tax. So that amendment was specifically aimed at the United States bonds. Now, the court... Aren't you here specifically aiming at government-derived proper interest, a government-derived interest? Yes, but... Well, does it make it any less so that you also cover some other exemption? Does that change the character of the general proposition of Miller against Milwaukee? Namely, that if you want to bring that pigeon down, you can't do it. It doesn't make a difference whether you bring the pigeon down from front or back. That's correct, Your Honor. That's the argument, isn't it? If the statute is aimed at the United States bonds and is not specifically, then it's an invalid tax. Now, of course, in our case, we contend that it is not aimed at the United States property. Because you also hit other pigeons. Pardon? Because you also hit the exemptions of Michigan health. That's right. And religious institutions. That's correct, Mr. Justice Black. So it gets down to a question largely on that point, Mr. Dodd, of whether there's a discriminatory classification. That's very true. And Carmichael v. Southern Coal and Coke Company, which I've cited at page 28 of my brief, and from which I quote, says this in connection with the taxing classes and with reference to exemptions. There are exemptions provided in this Act 189, which I will later discuss. Carmichael v. Southern Coal Company, decided by this court in 1937, and I quote therefrom as follows. It is inherent in the exercise of the power to tax that a state be free to select the subjects of taxation and to grant exemptions. Neither due process nor equal protection imposes upon a state any rigid rule of equality of taxation. This court has repeatedly held that inequalities which result from a singling out of one particular class for taxation or exemptions infringe no constitutional limitations, citing many cases. Like considerations govern exemptions from the operation of a tax imposed upon the members of a class. A legislature is not bound to tax every member of a class or none. It may make distinctions of degree, having a rational basis, and when subjected to judicial scrutiny, they must be presumed to rest on that basis if there is any conceivable state of facts which would support it. One more... Well, are there any exemptions in your statute? Pardon? Are there any exemptions in your statute? Yes. Does it include all? Is that a complete classification? A property of any state-supported educational institution is one of the exemptions in Act 189. You have one. Yes. There are two others, and the two are these. Where the use is by way of a concession in or relative to the use of a public airport, park, market, fairground, or other similar property, which is available to the use of the general public, and one more. In the case of federal property for which payments are made in lieu of taxes in amounts equivalent to taxes which might otherwise be lawfully assessed. Those provisions appear, I believe, in Section 1 of Act 189. Suppose, Mr. O'Connor, instead of this compendious provision... What's the name? What's the name of the statute? Oh, no. 189. 189. Suppose, instead of in the form in which we have it, Section 1 said all leaseholds from government, federal government immune properties shall be assessed on the value of the property for the privilege of having such a leasehold. Section 2, all leaseholds that were immune from taxation because owned by the state of Michigan shall be assessed, shall be taxed to the full value of such immunized state property. Section 3, all property derived, owned by a city when leased, etc. Section 4, all property of charitable religious organizations enjoying immunity as such. Suppose the statute is like that. Four sections. Putting in all the categories of property as such exempt for taxing the privilege of having a leasehold thereof. Would you be making the same argument? I would say this, if your honor, please. As we know, and as government counsel has pointed out, Section 6 of the Military Leasing Act of 1947 provides for the taxation of the lessee's interest as far as local taxing agencies are concerned. Now, I think we would have that right regardless of that provision. But we say here we are not taxing the lessee's interest. If we taxed the lessee's interest, then we would, under the language in the Allegheny case, be required to evaluate the lessee's interest in property in accordance with regularly accepted methods of appraisal, such as taking into consideration the term of the lease, the termination provisions in the lease, the amount of rent, and so forth. Now, we obviously didn't do that. The fact that the lessee's interest would have been on public property and put them on an equal footing for the reason that the lessee's interest would only amount to an infinitesimal part of the money that can be received in the fashion the legislature taxed provided in this act. Now, as I say, the legislature could have imposed a much larger sum. The fact that it is equal to the tax on the property does not make it a tax on the property because, again, as I say, a specific tax, and of course a specific tax, as your honors know, is nothing but an excise tax, and examples of which are occupation taxes, privilege taxes, and license taxes. Now, those taxes were placed upon the lessee's use of the property in connection to the business conducted for profit to put the lessees on an equal basis with lessees of private and public property. For example, Corporation A, coming into the state of Michigan, desires to lease property. It finds that I have a parcel of real estate, a private person, and it finds the government has a parcel of real estate. Both parcels meet their specifications to perfection. Which parcel will this corporation rent? Certainly not mine, because they know if they rent mine, they're going to have to pay taxes either in the amount of the rent charged or in addition to the rent charged in consideration of a reduction in that rent. And in that respect, it's very discriminatory. And it was that very thing that the legislature sought to eliminate in passing this act. Now, Flint v. Stone Tracy was a situation where the federal government sought to tax franchises of corporations in various states based upon and measured by the income of the corporation, including municipally tax-exempt bonds. Now, the federal government did not grant those franchises. If the federal government can do that in connection with state franchises not granted by it, then certainly the states ought to be able to tax a privilege of using which arises out of an instrument, namely the lease of the federal government. The fact that the privilege of using the property is exercised within the jurisdiction of the state of Michigan is sufficient in and of itself alone to permit the state to tax. And I have covered that point in my brief wherein I say, in connection with home insurance company case, which quotes from Savings v. Coit, nothing can be more certain in legal decisions than that the privileges and franchises of a private corporation in all trades and avocations by which the citizens acquire a livelihood may be taxed by a state for the support of a state governor. The authority to that effect resides in the state independent of the federal government and is wholly unaffected by the fact that the corporation or individual has or has not made investment in federal securities. One other point I would like to raise, counsel for the government refers to the Senate Committee hearings and refers to Section 6 of the Military Leasing Act. We say it does not apply because we're not taxing the lessee's interest. The Military Leasing Act does not prohibit the taxing of a privilege of using the property. There was no discussions in the Senate Committee hearings in connection with the privilege of using the property. And while the Army and Navy, as I gather from a reading of the Senate report, were both interested in seeing that properties leased by the government for commercial purposes should be taxed in order to eliminate that discrimination that is ever present between public and private lessees. They were not able to arrive at any legal basis for doing it. As one of the Senators I recall said, when it was suggested that you transfer title of the government to the lessee during the term of the lease, one of the Senators said, I don't think that would be constitutional because you cannot place ownership in a person that actually doesn't own the property by a congressional act. Therefore, they forgot it, decided to leave it to general legislation, but as a last measure, passed Section 6 of the Military Leasing Act, which only infinitesimally helps in the situation to avoid discrimination. It doesn't because you don't get the same results as you would from a lessee of private property. I see my time is up. Your Honors, please. Mr. Street, we'll finish. Mr. Street, Senator Hunter, please the court. I don't want to labor this too long, but there are a few issues that are unique to our particular situation being Continental Motors Corporation located in Muskegon County. and a few points that I would like to attempt to clarify. It's quite apparent from reading opposing counsel's brief that they refuse to make a distinction between a property tax and a privilege tax, refuse to concede that this might conceivably be a privilege tax rather than a property tax, and treat it that way throughout. Both their original brief and their reply brief. I might say our reply brief, the reply brief, was only received yesterday. I'll try to cover it in oral argument to save filing a reply to the reply if we can do so. I think it'll clarify the picture somewhat if we point out some of the instances in which Act 189 does not apply. Post office is a prime example. It could never apply to a post office. There's some mention made in the footnote of the reply brief that it might apply to the Pentagon building, that Virginia might tax the secretary for occupying the Pentagon building. Of course, that could never happen under one Act 89, and I don't think it could happen under any other. The very simple reason he is not a private individual or corporation who is using the property in connection with a business conducted for profit. So the same is, of course, true of an army camp, a marine base, any installation of the sort that's not used for profit, it could never apply. Some reference has been made to forest preserves, grazing lands. I might point out, too, if those are public lands open to the public in the nature of a park, and the government grants a privilege by way of a concession to someone to graze those lands, it again would not come within the Act because of the express exception, as long as that land is, again, open to use by the public, and that's an important feature of the Act. We have a forest preserve in Michigan, and perhaps we can explain this a little more clearly as to just what might happen. The Manistee Forest Preserve is a short distance north of Muskegon. It is not taxable. It places some burdens upon our local government, but certainly not unreasonable burdens, and we don't care to tax it. But what if the government should lease that land to be timbered? We know what happens in Michigan well enough when such leases are made. A large mill is brought in that brings in hundreds of employees, and they bring their families. They must be housed. Their children must be schooled. Roads must be built and fire protection afforded. Then we have an entirely different situation. I say that private entrepreneur who is harvesting the trees from that land from profit should be taxed on his privilege, and this court has held that he may be taxed. I'd like to refer to Wilson v. Cook, where there was an Arkansas statute which imposed a privilege on anyone engaged in the business of severing from the soil for commercial purposes, natural resources, including timber. In this particular instance, it was a forest preserve. The trees belonged to the United States government as well as the land. This man was given a contract to sever the trees. He enjoyed a privilege granted exclusively by the federal government to harvest these trees. yet a severance tax imposed by the state of Arkansas was upheld by this court on the basis of James v. Dravo and other cases. Act 189 would effect substantially the same thing in this case if these forest preserves were leased for that purpose, and it's only just that it should do so. There's some claim that Continental stands in a little different status here than Borg-Werner because Borg-Werner is manufacturing automobile parts for profit, while Continental is confined to manufacturing tank engines for the Army Corps. There is some difference on the surface there, it's true. You want to keep in mind, however, that Continental is in competition with Chrysler, General Motors, and Ford who also like to make engines and who are at a distinct disadvantage in competing with Continental. We don't mind that in Muskegon, but I say in the long run anything that removes this spur of free competition is going to work detrimental to this government who may think temporarily they are getting a bargain by giving Continental the plant rent-free and tax-free. The claim is also made that Continental because of this unusual situation is an agent or instrumentality of the government and they're sure of course should be tax exempt. That situation I think is covered in the case cited in my brief of Hennersburg v. Silas Mason and I don't know as I need to elaborate it further here. That same contention was made in lower court and ultimately abandoned on appeal. But what if we did even for the sake of argument concede that Continental in this particular case is an agent or instrumentality of the federal government does it afford an immunity under the decisions of this court? I might point out that in United States v. California which is of course familiar to you and is included in an ALR citation in my brief in referring to this restriction or immunity says it's equally a restriction on taxation by either of the instrumentalities of the other. The state instrumentalities supposedly enjoy the same privilege. But what have been some of the decisions? The early case of South Carolina followed up later by Ohio v. Helvring where the state owned liquor sold it through its own dispensaries. This court imposed a privilege tax upon the sale of that liquor and held it valid. The court used this rather colorful language. When the state enters the marketplace seeking customers it divests itself of its quasi-sovereignty. Quotato. Even more closely at home when the state of New York owning the Saratoga Springs attempted to sell water through its own public commission the federal government imposed a tax of two cents per gallon upon the water. This court sustained the tax saying that it is clear that where a state engages in a business in competition with private enterprise it enjoys no special privilege or immunity. And even closer to home is Allen versus University system where Georgia set up a state commission to operate the University of Georgia and Georgia Tech and they were held liable for the admission tax to the football games though conceding that that was a part of an educational function and that education was a proper function of the state yet that tax was imposed and sustained. I don't believe first that Continental is an agent or instrumentality of the federal government but if so because of its peculiar activity I don't believe it's entitled to any immunity particularly. Now much is made here of the measure of the tax in fact it's about the only argument made against it saying since it's measured on the basis of the value of the property that it therefore amounts to a tax on the property itself. How could such a tax be measured and really be fair and just? It is suggested that perhaps if it were measured on something like oh we'll say in the case about the severance of trees on a board foot basis or in the S.O. case where you sustained a tax of six cents per gallon on S.O. for storing government owned gasolines that perhaps if it were measured by gallons or something of that sort it would be a different picture and wouldn't look like a tax on the property. But how could it be done? Acres is the only thing that might come to mind as being some standard of that sort. But how would acres apply? The three and a half acres upon which this eight million dollar plant rests in Muskegon County, why a tax of $10,000 per acre clearly would be reasonable. But there's for instance a 20 acre tract adjoining that's used as nothing for a testing ground which is virtually vacant land, that land wouldn't be worth $200 an acre and below it is a three acre partial use to dump waste that's not worth $10 an acre. Certainly you cannot arrive at a fair and just tax on any other basis than the measure that the state of Michigan sought bit to employ here. Council's reply brief is directed at two things, the Military Leasing Act and the other. It's repeated over and over again that the use is included in the privilege. I mean rather that the use is included in the lease, the privilege of use is included in the lease, whether the lease be one year, five years, or ten. The privilege of use is also included in ownership you want to keep in mind. And it has been held that we can segregate the faggots and tax them separately. But the burden of the argument there is that since the privilege of use is necessarily included within a lease or even ownership, it can never be taxed up to the same amount as a tax that might be imposed because of ownership or because of a leasehold interest viewing it as a property right. Now that simply is not the case. In fact, it may be taxed far in excess of that amount. Let's look at the gasoline stored by Esso Standard Oil, for which they paid six cents a gallon for the privilege of storing. Now if Esso had owned that gasoline themselves and had it in their own tanks, they wouldn't have been subject to the tax because they would not have been engaged in the prisoners of storing gasoline. They would have paid irregular ad valorem personal property tax by virtue of their ownership at the end of the year. What would it have amounted to? Possibly 10, 15 mils. Six mils on gasoline worth possibly 30 or 35 cents a gallon is somewhere around 150 mils. Now, a man who owns furs and has them in a warehouse will pay an ad valorem personal property tax of a few mils on it each year. But if he elects to exercise his privilege, which is included in his privilege of ownership, of sale during a year, immediately a sales tax in Michigan of 3% or 30 mils is imposed. And his troubles are only beginning because the federal government then imposes a 10% tax, which is 100 mils, because he exercised his privilege of sale, which is included within his ownership, so that the tax upon a privilege may far exceed any tax that can be imposed because of ownership alone. In this instance, it's merely made equal. The interesting part to me about this long reference to the Military Leasing Act, lies in the debate that it is recognized that a serious injustice and inequality exists. The long years of debate that have gone on in the Senate and in Congress results, really, in nothing. We've labored at a mountain and come up with a molehill here. They all say it's a serious problem. It's unjust. Something ought to be done. But what should be done? What can we do that will bring about a fair and just solution? The inference is they've virtually given up except for one thing, they're going to resort to a federal dole in the payments and what they call payments in lieu of taxes. Now, some reference has been made to the fact that the school district I represent has been forced to accept some of those. Some material here did not apply in the year 1954, and they did not receive any for that year. There has been a temporary act passed since, which expires in 1958, which for our purposes will expire next year because our tax for 57 isn't payable until 58. We may have one more year under that act, but we don't know whether it will be extended or not. I think we'll all agree that this federal dole is certainly an unsatisfactory solution in any extent. Is it the general act that expires this? Yes, it's general, quite broad in its scope. At least it covers the continental plant. At least it covers the continental plant. What is the general act? In this particular act, as I recall, it's land that formerly belonged to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and then fell into government. It all relates to Reconstruction Finance property. This particular act, as I recall, it applies in our case. There are other acts that do apply, but they don't apply in all things such as here in 1954. There was no applicable act. I know there's present, are there applicable acts for police holds made today, this year. Are they covered by acts? Are they all covered? Well, I know there's a military leasing act, and that of course would get to be a small tax if the lease is one year or terminable at will, and so on. The point I want to make here, well, here was the main problem that pointed out, as you'll notice in Senate debate. One senator said, well, let's transfer title over to these people, and with a recapture clause. That'll make it taxable, and that'll solve our problem. Someone pointed out the situation, though, and it was referred to here. The government may want to reserve a large part of that plant for storage, and on the lease will say a third. Well, the lessee, if he's going to get taxed on the whole property, won't like that. Act 189 takes care of that. It's only the property actually used, that's made available to and actually used. Now, there was some inference made that perhaps in the Board Warner case, some space used for storage was included in the assessment. If so, it was by error and could have been corrected had it been called the attention to assessing officers, I'm sure, because that portion of the plant would not be used. Another problem with confrontor them, what we might refer to as white elephant plants. Here's a big plant that costs millions of dollars to build. We want it as a standby facility. It doesn't have too much value for commercial use, and yet if we transfer title over, it'll be taxed at full value. That's taken care of, too, in this sort of a situation. Let's look at Continental Plant, a value of $8 million to cost. It's on the assessment rolls at $3 million. Our assessor recognizes and must assess property in the state of Michigan on the basis of its present market value, what it will bring on the market today, which equalizes something and copes with the problem that I say cannot be solved on a federal level. Now, the whole attitude seems to have been here by opposing counsel. Well, the United States Congress has coped with this matter for a great many years and has not received and obtained a solution, which they might do sometime in the future. But in the meantime, let's get along with this dole or something. We've done everything that can be done. Now, with all due respect to the United States Congress, I don't believe that they have a monopoly on wisdom. I think there's a little residue of wisdom left in the Michigan state legislature. And instead of debating on ad infinitum, the Michigan legislature has done something. And the unique part of it here is no one comes here and says that this act is unfair to the United States government, that it's unfair to Continental Motors or to Borg Warner, or that it's unfair to anyone else. Both of the lower courts commented on the inherent justice and desirability of the act, and no one has pointed out any inherent evil. Some comment has been made that the act is a little artistic and not sophisticated. I think that's one of its best merits. It's a very simple act. We make use of existing machinery that's already in operation. We don't have to set up a new bureau with a lot of new elaborate employees to administer this act. It's simple in its operation, it's clear in its understand, and it's equitable in its operation. Your Honor, I always ask is this court considers that in view of the reply brief, the action taken there, that it's entirely possible that the legislature of the state of Michigan, in using this residue of wisdom that's left of them, have solved a problem, at least on a local level, which I submit cannot be solved on a federal level. Thank you, Your Honor. Mr. Street, in your township of Muskegon, how do you assess this property? Do you assess it as personal property, or does it go on the real property role, as we were told? This one slipped on the real property role. This one got on the real property role. It was pointed out this was a new act. The assessors didn't know just what to do with it. In our township, this property had been carried on the assessment role right along, you see, until it was ultimately declared surplus and went through various channels, and then in 1953, the year this act became effective, went to the United States as such. So the assessor already had it on his role. So he simply went ahead and made an assessed value and set it down, in this instance, on the real property role. It seems to me I don't see any substance to the difference. Technically, there probably should be a third role set up for this type of property, I agree. May I ask, Mr. Streep, I gather in striking the tax rate, you aggregate both real property assessments and personal property tax assessments, does it? This act does not apply to personal property care. Speaking generally, in striking the local tax rate, you have a uniform rate that applies both to real estate assessments and personal property tax assessments. Yes, the mechanics of the way it's done in Michigan is the assessor goes out and evaluates all the property into this. Real or personal? Real or personal, yes. And then finds out what the school must have, county must have, and so on. And then decides what millage must be applied to that valuation to produce the amount of money needed. That's the mechanics of it. So that you have the same rate, the consequences, you get the same rate, whether the tax is on personal property or on real property. Yes, that is correct. The same rate, and in arriving at that rate, you aggregate the assessments against real property and the assessments against personal property all together. You lump them all together, yes. And then strike the rate from that. That's correct. So it doesn't practically make any difference whether this assessment is listed on a personal property tax rule or a real estate tax rule or otherwise. Not a particle or on a third tax rule. It all comes out the same place, yes. Mr. Streak, you said several times this can't be dealt with by Congress. It must be dealt with locally. If that's so, that, for me at least, would have a very important bearing on striking the adjustment between state and federal authority. Why do you say that? One where the difficulty is pointed out. About the only way it could be done on a federal level would be to transfer this title back with a recapture clause. Well, just an authorization by Congress to let each state do what Michigan tried to do would do it, wouldn't it?
